Des comptoirs contre l’insécurité alimen: Food counters to fight food insecurity
C’est d’abord le besoin, puis l’indignat: First it was need, then indignation, that led Atlantide Desrochers to take on the issue of food waste.
Atlantide Desroches, fondatrice de Solid: Atlantide Desroches, founder of Solidarité & Partage, at the food counter at the Centre du Plateau. Photo: Pablo Ortiz
C’est d’abord le besoin, puis l’indignat: First it was need, then indignation, that led Atlantide Desrochers to take on the issue of food waste. Five years later, at the head of a citizen movement that has become a non-profit organization, the Plateau Mont-Royal resident intends to take the fight beyond her neighbourhood. Partage et Solidarité collects surplus food every day and redistributes it each week at six (soon seven) food counters. It is early afternoon and, in the middle of a space buzzing with activity, the food is piling up ahead of the coming distribution. It's hard to believe there will be nothing left in a few hours. Yet that's what the founder tells us, explaining how this sharing initiative got off the ground, and how its success shows how necessary it is.
<strong>Mme Desrochers, comment en êtes-: Ms. Desrochers, how did you come to start Partage et solidarité?
Ce n’était pas du tout prévu dans mon pa: It wasn't planned at all in my path. I was going through a hard time, and I saw how much resources could be lacking. While looking for solutions, I became aware of the waste, discovering among other things what was in the garbage when I was out walking with my kids. I created Partage et Solidarité somewhat by accident. In the first year, I didn't have an organization, but there were shopkeepers who gave me products. I set up a fridge at home, the Frigo Plateau. A year later, I created the fridge at the Cabane de l'amitié, with the Centre communautaire de l'amitié. Slowly, with the fridge, it turned into distribution. I opened the first counter in 2018. Now there are six. Every month we distribute 2,000 community baskets, made up of bread, vegetables, and vegetarian and vegan products, which feed 8,000 people. We're talking about 41 businesses taking part, including supermarkets. That's a real first, since several of them had exclusivity deals with other organizations. Between the donations, it would be a shame for this food to go nowhere.
<strong>Comment opèrent les comptoirs al: How do the Partage et Solidarité food counters work?
Ce sont des comptoirs mobiles. On arrive: They're mobile counters. We show up, and when we leave, there's no trace of us left. People just have to book an appointment, through Facebook, by email or on our website – it's very simple. They just have to give their name and tell us how many people are in the household so we can make baskets that match the size of the family. Then they just have to show up. At a food bank, access is restricted. They ask for a lot of information. People have to tell their whole story and show their tax return from the previous year to get anything. Sometimes they're even asked how they ended up there. Some don't dare go back; it puts them in awful situations. I found that to be complete nonsense. It's important to understand that anyone can go through bad times. Nobody is safe from a mishap or from problems. So these counters are here for everyone, whether you're going through a rough patch that's temporary or one that lasts longer. Anyone who feels they need food is welcome. There's no questionnaire or form to fill out. We pick up products in the morning, and we sort and distribute in the afternoon. Every day we're in a different place; we share spaces. We show up, collect food in a neighbourhood and give it back to people in that neighbourhood. The idea is to create local infrastructure, run by people from the neighbourhood. The people behind the project are residents who want to see improvements there. We could do this in every neighbourhood if we had more resources. There are 5 employees and 70 volunteers. Everyone who comes to volunteer with us receives two grocery bags of food that they choose themselves. Some handle administrative support or do outreach, especially to shopkeepers, and others help us find grants.

<strong>Quelles ont été les répercussion: What impact did COVID-19 have on food distribution?
Je n’ai jamais demandé de justificatif ;: I never asked for proof; I've even lost potential funders because I didn't want to ask people for it. All we need to know is whether people are there or not. With COVID-19, it became acceptable. It changed the dynamic; the project became more legitimate. The government and the public understood that it can happen to anyone, to lose your job, to have money troubles, to not be able to make ends meet. It became much more visible. Demand went up, and the reality is that we created new counters. And at every counter, demand exploded. My priority is that people eat all year round, but it's very hard in January and February. After the holidays. We have to think about it a lot; those are very tough months. Fruit and vegetables are harder to get, much harder to get in winter. We have to go to more stores. We have to remember that some people can't get around as easily, even though they need food. As long as there's snow, people need a lot more support. We see a lot of seniors and families. The atmosphere has been harder since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.
<strong>Plusieurs initiatives ont témoig: Several initiatives have spoken of how hard it is to get donations from shopkeepers. How should one go about it?
J’ai préparé une <l1>consultation publiq: I prepared a <l1>public consultation</l1> on this issue, so that everyone is aware of the situation and so that the people and organizations who want to recover food know that there are tools. I wrote <l2>a brief</l2> that explains everything that can be done in Quebec and elsewhere. Shopkeepers are much more complicated. They want to give, they don't like throwing things out. The problem is all the work that has to be done around it. You have to say that we're not asking them for a favour, we're offering them a service. We take their unsold goods, everything that's still good. For stores, it's big savings. The business wouldn't have to get rid of its surplus stock as often. For example, we're talking about 20, 25 crates a day at a supermarket we visit. I insist on the fact that we're not going begging. We offer a pickup and distribution service that the shopkeeper doesn't have to manage. Partage et Solidarité is a charity, and a shopkeeper can, if they wish, receive a receipt for their donation. Often they're super busy and have a lot to manage. If we don't give them the tools, if we don't tell them that we'll be there, that we're punctual, that we have our own crates, that it's publicity for them, that it saves them money and that we'll give them a charity receipt if they want one, they might listen. It has to become more and more normal. When I approached shopkeepers five years ago, it was pretty complicated. Today, some of them are waiting for me, so we've come a long way. When I first approached them, I was holding my baby in my arms. I was outraged. I pointed the cameras to show the public what was in the garbage. I took a lot of photos to post on social media, asking how it is that this is being thrown out. I encouraged people to help me, and that's how it worked. I started from the principle that it's more normal to give than to throw away.
<strong>Il y a plusieurs comptoirs sur l: There are several counters in the Plateau. Do people have a false idea of the borough?
Le Plateau, ce n’est pas uniquement ce q: The Plateau isn't only what people think. For example, I live in a family housing co-op, on a very sought-after street in the Plateau, where there are very spacious houses. My kids go to the same school as children from well-off families, along with others who live in public housing (HLM). You can see it, these are different lives. Because it's a school in a wealthy neighbourhood, there's no funding for snacks, for example. Day camps cost double what camps in other neighbourhoods do. Since I have three kids, it would have cost me more than I earned in a week, so I brought them to work with me. That's the reality for a lot of people. Poverty in the Plateau is hard to live with. There are also very expensive businesses, so it's hard to be poor in the Plateau – everything around is expensive. Still, we want to go outside the neighbourhood. There's a counter in Centre-Sud, which is a first step. I tried other neighbourhoods, but it didn't work out; I couldn't find space. In March, I'm opening a new counter in Côte-des-Neiges.
<strong>De quoi Partage et Solidarité a-: What does Partage et Solidarité need most right now?
Sur le plan du matériel, c’est difficile: In terms of equipment, it's tough. We went from two to six counters in a year and a half, and we have only one truck for 15 tonnes of food. It's tight. We always need volunteers, but above all, we need shopkeepers to give. They play an essential role. People who can afford it can make a financial donation. That lets us pay our employees and keep the truck running. Support on social media is also very important to us.

Atlantide Desrochers a déposé une pétiti: Atlantide Desrochers submitted a petition with more than 15,000 signatures to the City of Montréal. This initiative led to a public consultation on December 3, 2020. Last April, the environment commission presented its official recommendations (21). These include a ban on the destruction of unsold goods starting in 2022 and a requirement for all merchants to enter into a food recovery agreement by 2025.
À la suite d’une autre consultation publ: Following another public consultation, the City of Montréal is proposing in its 2020-2025 Residual Materials Management Plan to cut food waste by 50% by 2025.
Mme Desroches a déposé une pétition cont: Ms. Desroches submitted a petition against food waste to the National Assembly in 2019 with the support of Ruba Ghazal, MNA for Mercier.
